title: People With Numbers
tagline: A British champion saw a man learn a pack of cards on television and went on to win the world title eight times. His system turns every pair of digits into a famous person.
card: The system that turns number pairs into people and actions, made by an eight-times world champion, and why a person is easier to hold than a word.
goal: you will learn the Dominic System letter code, turn number pairs into people, and use the rule that one person plus another person's action can hold four digits.

left_off.q: What are the sounds for 1, 2, 3 and 4 in the Major System?

left_off.a: Vowels, w, h and y carry no digit, so you can add them to make real words.

left_off.q: What number does the word MOON stand for?

story.heading: The man who learned a pack of cards on television

text: In 1987 a young Englishman called Dominic O'Brien was watching television when a man appeared who could memorise the order of a shuffled pack of cards. The presenter shuffled, the man looked at each card once, and then he named the whole pack in order, without a mistake.
O'Brien did not think of himself as someone with a special memory. That evening he did something unusual. He picked up a pack of cards and tried to find out how the trick was done.

check.q: What happened in 1987 to change O'Brien's mind?
check.a: He saw someone memorise a shuffled pack of cards on television, and decided to find out how it was done.

parts.talk: Have you ever seen someone do something that made you say 'I could learn that'? What was it?

text: He read about the old methods: the places, the pictures, the stories. He trained, and he made up his own ways of speeding it up. In 1991 he won the first World Memory Championship, in London. He went on to win it eight times in all.

In 2002 he memorised fifty-four decks of cards, in a single viewing of each, a record that made the newspapers: 2,808 cards in total. He did it with the same two tools you have already learned, a long route of places and strong pictures. He also built a way of turning numbers into people.

check.a: The first World Memory Championship in 1991, and eight world titles in all.

parts.talk: What do you think was the hardest part of his training: making the pictures, or learning the places?

text: His idea is that a person is the best picture there is. A word like toes is a picture, but you meet it and forget it. A person has a face, a voice, a way of moving, and things they do. If every pair of digits is a famous person doing something, then a long number becomes a short film, and a film is far easier to remember than a row of digits.
This system is named for him. It is the system behind the PAO method of the next room, and it is the link between the simple systems of room 6 and the champion's methods of rooms 21 and 23.

check.q: Why does O'Brien use famous people for numbers?
check.a: A person is rich in detail: face, voice, movement and action, so a person is a stronger picture than a plain word.

parts.talk: Which famous person do you find easiest to picture, and what is the first thing you see them doing?

words.m: the first letter of a name. Albert Einstein has the initials A. E.
something a person does. Directing a film is an action.
the best result ever achieved. A world record.
to learn something so that you can remember it exactly.

source: O'Brien's career and records are summarised from public accounts. The Dominic System is his own invention; the details below are told in our own words.
method_heading: Digits to letters, letters to people

method.x: Every digit becomes a letter. A pair of digits becomes a pair of initials. The initials belong to a person you can see, and that person has one famous action.

Why these letters? 1 to 5 simply follow the alphabet. After that: an S looks like a 6, a G looks a little like a 7, the letter H says aitch, which sounds like eight, N is the first letter of nine, and O looks like a zero.

items.h: Turn each digit into a letter.
Find a person with those initials.
items.x: A. O. = Al Oerter (an Olympic discus champion). S. S. = Steven Spielberg.
Oerter: throwing a discus. Spielberg: directing a film.

items.h: Four digits = one person + another's action.
items.x: Take the person of the first pair and the action of the second pair.

try.title: Pair to initials
try.prompt: Match each pair of digits to its initials.

try.title: Encode 1776
try.prompt: Split 1776 into 17 and 76. 17 is A. G. (for example Al Gore). 76 is G. S. (for example Gene Simmons of the band Kiss, sticking out his tongue). Write the scene: the person of 17 doing the action of 76 at the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
try.model: Al Gore is at the signing of the Declaration of Independence in 1776, sticking out his tongue at the delegates while they sign. The quills scratch and a drum rolls.
checks: I used the person of the first pair.
I used the action of the second pair.
I put it in a scene about the event.

try.title: Encode 1945
try.prompt: 1945: 19 = A. N. (for example Alfred Nobel), 45 = E. D. (for example Emily Dickinson, writing a poem). Make a scene for the end of the Second World War.
try.model: Alfred Nobel is sitting in the ruins of a city writing a poem about peace on a piece of paper that is also a white flag. People are cheering.
checks: It is connected to the event.

try.title: Choose your own
try.prompt: Pick a pair you have not seen yet (for example 29 or 55 or 99). Write the initials, find a famous person and give them one clear action. If you cannot think of anyone, use someone from your own life.
try.model: There is no single answer. For example, 55 = E. E.: Emma ..., or a friend. The test is whether you can see them doing something.

try.q: For the number 4321, which person and action do you use?
try.why: Person of the first pair, action of the second: the person of 43 (D. C.) doing the action of 21 (B. A.).

try.title: Say it aloud
try.prompt: Say your own 1776 and 1945 scenes aloud. Then say which digits each person and each action stands for.

quiz.q: In the Dominic System, four digits are held by...
quiz.why: The person of the first pair, the action of the second.

quiz.q: Who is 15 in the starter list?
Which has more initials to match?
quiz.why: A pair gives two initials, the person's first and last name.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: seven people
challenge.intro: These seven people stand for the pairs 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17 and 18. Learn them in order. Say the pair and the initials as you see each person.
challenge.study: Place each person in a place along your palace route, doing their action.

look_back.q: What does the Major System code use to stand for digits?
look_back.a: Consonant sounds, one for each digit. Vowels are free.

look_back.q: What number is the word BIKE?
Name the shape picture for 8 and the rhyme picture for 8.
How can a story chain and a palace work together?
look_back.a: A short chain at each place: the palace holds the order, the chain the detail.
